paper_metadata.title: Multicompartmental models and diffusion abnormalities in paediatric mild traumatic brain injury

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used a large, prospective cohort design with consecutive recruitment from clinical settings. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are clearly defined, and the baseline sample is well-described, including matching for age and sex.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients (8–18 years of age) were consecutively recruited from local emergency department and urgent care settings between July 2016 and February 2020
items.reasoning: The authors specify the age range, recruitment source (ED/Urgent Care), and timeframe.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: consecutively recruited patients (n = 203; 8-18 years old) and age and sex-matched healthy controls (n = 170) in a prospective cohort design.
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment in a prospective design is the gold standard for limiting selection bias in prognosis studies.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between July 2016 and February 2020
items.reasoning: Specific dates are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: local emergency department and urgent care settings... University of New Mexico Institutional Review Board
items.reasoning: The setting (ED/Urgent care) and general location (implied by the University affiliation) are clear.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria were based on both American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine (upper threshold) and Zurich Concussion in Sport Group (lower threshold), and included Glasgow Coma Score ≥13, LOC (if present) limited to 30 min, PTA (limited to 24 h)
items.reasoning: Criteria are based on established clinical guidelines with specific thresholds for GCS, LOC, and PTA.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: The final SA sample (Supplementary material and Fig. 1) included 204 pmTBI... and 173 matched HC
items.reasoning: The sample size is large for a neuroimaging study, and the flowchart (Fig 1) suggests systematic enrollment.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The pmTBI and HC groups did not differ in terms of handedness, age, self-reported Tanner stage of development and biological sex (all P-values ≥ 0.429; see Supplementary Table 2).
items.reasoning: Key demographic and developmental characteristics are reported and compared between groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Retention was high (>80% for patients), and the authors explicitly compared completers to non-completers, finding no significant differences that would suggest informative censoring.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 152 pmTBI... (81.3% retention without individuals excluded from study) and 155 HC (95.5% retention without study excludes) returned for the second visit.
items.reasoning: Retention of 81.3% in the patient group meets the standard threshold for low risk of bias.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not explicitly describe specific outreach methods for those who did not return.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Fig. 1 presents a flowchart of enrolment, inclusion and data quality control
items.reasoning: While the flowchart accounts for exclusions (e.g., data quality), specific personal reasons for patient dropout are not detailed in the main text.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics
items.reasoning: The authors state they checked for associations between attrition and key characteristics.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Loss to follow-up... is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample)
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly confirm that the analyzed sample represents the baseline sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses advanced, objective neuroimaging (dMRI) with standardized protocols and biologically informed modeling. The measurement is consistent across all participants.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: High angular resolution dMRI scans were acquired using a twice-refocused spin-echo sequence with 165 diffusion-weighted gradients
items.reasoning: The prognostic factors (dMRI metrics) are defined by the technical acquisition parameters.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: All data were collected at the same imaging centre and on the same machine, reducing concerns about inter-scanner and vendor-related differences
items.reasoning: Single-scanner protocols and advanced preprocessing (TOPUP/EDDY) enhance reliability.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise dMRI analyses (AFNI's 3dLME module) were conducted
items.reasoning: The study uses continuous voxel-wise data rather than arbitrary dichotomization.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All data were collected at the same imaging centre and on the same machine
items.reasoning: Standardization is explicitly stated.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Fig. 1... inclusion and data quality control
items.reasoning: The flowchart indicates that only participants with usable dMRI data were included in the final analysis.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not mention imputation for dMRI data; it appears cases with poor quality data were excluded.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes include standardized clinical assessments and cognitive batteries. Assessors (neuroradiologists) were blinded, and the timing of follow-up was consistent.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Data collection occurred during SA (1–11 days post-injury) and early chronic (EC, ∼4 months post-injury) injury phases.
items.reasoning: The timing and nature of outcomes (PCS, cognitive scores) are well-defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Structural magnetic resonance images were reviewed by a board-certified neuroradiologist blinded to participant group
items.reasoning: Blinding of the neuroradiologist and use of validated batteries (PROMIS, PCSI) support validity.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A Common Data Elements battery... was administered at both visits
items.reasoning: Standardized administration for all participants.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study rigorously accounts for confounding through matching (age/sex), statistical adjustment (age-at-injury, motion, reading ability, effort), and sensitivity analyses.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: age, self-reported Tanner stage... history of previous head injuries, parental self-reported psychopathology, maximum parental education, premorbid reading ability... and effort
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of demographic, developmental, and psychological confounders was measured.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: age at first visit (unit = months; equivalent to age-at-injury) as a covariate
items.reasoning: Confounders like age are precisely defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Wide Range Achievement Test 4 (WRAT4)... Test of Memory Malingering—10-item short version (TOMMe10)
items.reasoning: Validated psychometric tools were used for key confounders like reading ability and effort.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A Common Data Elements battery... was administered at both visits
items.reasoning: Consistency in measurement across groups.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not specify how missing confounder data was handled.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: HC were recruited to match based on age and sex
items.reasoning: Matching was used in the design phase.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: age-at-injury and mean framewise displacement entered as additional covariates
items.reasoning: Multivariable adjustment was used for both biological and technical (motion) confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis is sophisticated, using mixed-factor models, machine learning, and cross-validation. Multiple comparison corrections were applied, and the strategy was pre-specified.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise dMRI analyses (AFNI's 3dLME module) were conducted with 2×2 [Group (HC versus pmTBI) × Visit (SA versus EC)] mixed factor models
items.reasoning: The statistical approach is detailed and transparent.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Biologically informed multicompartmental models... were also computed
items.reasoning: The use of MDT models was based on a clear biological rationale to improve upon standard NODDI assumptions.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise diffusion results were corrected using both parametric (P ≤ 0.001) and minimum volume thresholds
items.reasoning: Appropriate use of LME for longitudinal data and rigorous cluster-wise correction for imaging.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical and imaging results are reported for main effects of Group, Group × Visit, Group × Age and Group × Visit ×Age interactions.
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant interactions across all metrics.
